title: Seven in every moment
hook: contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life, attention: present in every mind-moment

segments.voice: Yesterday, cetasika, the mental factors. Your line: what colors the mind. When a mood showed up, could you call it a factor instead of yourself? Day one thousand seventy-three.

A king once asked a monk to do something impossible. The king was Milinda, the monk was Nagasena, and their long conversation was written down as the Questions of King Milinda. Nagasena had been naming what happens in the mind in a single moment: contact, feeling, perception, intention, and more. So the king pushed. Can you pull them apart? Show me this one here, and that one over there. Nagasena answered him with a kitchen.
screen: `A KING AND A MONK.` → `PULL THEM APART?` → `AN ANSWER FROM THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Suppose, he said, the royal cook makes a sauce, with curds and salt and ginger and pepper. If the king said, bring me just the taste of the salt, could the cook do it? No. Every flavor is really there, each with its own character, but none can be lifted out alone. That is today's picture. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha names seven mental factors present in every moment of consciousness, whatever kind it is: kind or cruel, sharp or sleepy. Here they are, plainly. Contact, phassa: the mind meets its object, like two hands meeting in a clap. Feeling, vedana: that meeting has a tone, pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Perception, sanna: the object is recognized and marked, this is blue, this is my sister's voice. Intention, cetana: the mind leans and organizes, aiming somewhere. One-pointedness: it rests on one object, even for an instant. The life faculty: what keeps the others going for as long as the moment lasts. And attention, manasikara: the mind turned toward this rather than that. Seven, in a moment of reading a street sign, a moment of anger, a moment of compassion. That is what makes the list useful. Feeling is in every moment, so no moment is without some tone. Intention is in every moment, so the mind is always leaning somewhere, even when it seems idle. And attention is always pointed, so the question is never whether the mind is attending, only to what. The sauce can't be separated in the bowl. The Abhidhamma names its parts anyway, not to take the sauce apart, but so more of it can be tasted.
screen: `THE SAUCE CAN'T BE UNMIXED.` · `SEVEN IN EVERY MOMENT.` · `ALWAYS A TONE, ALWAYS A LEAN.` · then, large: `NAMED, SO MORE CAN BE TASTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: contact and feeling. Rest one hand on your knee or on a table. Notice the moment it touches. That's contact. And with it, a tone: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Lift the hand and set it down again. Contact, and a tone. Then try it with a sound in the room, and then with the breath at the nostrils. Each time, just two things: it touched, and it had a tone. No need to hunt for the other five. They are there whether you find them or not. The bell holds the time.
Seven in every moment. Contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life and attention: the factors the manual finds in every moment of mind. Today's word.
Your line: seven always. Today, three times, catch the tone of one moment: pleasant, unpleasant or neither. A sip of coffee, a phone buzzing, a doorway. Day one thousand seventy-three.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the seven universal factors by their Pali names, and some insight meditation teachers ask students to notice contact and the tone of feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, as it arises.

myth: the seven factors appear only in calm, wholesome moments
the manual finds them in every moment of consciousness: kind or cruel, sharp or sleepy.
Nagasena compares the factors in a moment to the flavors in a sauce
every flavor is there, but no one can lift out just the salt.
here, feeling means an emotion like sadness
vedana here is the tone of a moment: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither.

fork.setup: you're the royal cook. the king asks for only the taste of the salt from a finished sauce. what do you do?
options: strain the sauce until only the salt is left.
say it can't be done: the flavors are mixed.
bring him a spoonful of plain salt instead.
fork.reveal: in the Questions of King Milinda, Nagasena says the cook couldn't do it. each flavor is real and distinct, and none comes out alone. the factors in a moment are like that.

original.note: Pali phassa: contact, the first of the seven factors in every moment.

trapdoor: what you thought: some moments of mind are simple.
what it means: every moment has contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life and attention.
what a scholar hears: the Abhidhammattha Sangaha calls these seven common to every consciousness; Milinda's sauce shows why they are named but never found apart.

sources.ref: Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ch. 2 (the seven universal mental factors)
Milindapanha II.3 (the cook's sauce: separating the mental qualities; Rhys Davids, SBE XXXV, 1890)

notes: The seven universals (phassa, vedana, sanna, cetana, ekaggata, jivitindriya, manasikara) are from Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 2. The one-line glosses are plain-English paraphrases; confirm, especially 'the life faculty keeps the others going'.

Milindapanha: the sauce simile (curds, salt, ginger, pepper and more; the king cannot be brought the taste of the salt alone) is paraphrased. Confirm the section reference in Rhys Davids' SBE XXXV and the list of ingredients.
The clapping-hands image for contact is the writer's own, not presented as a source simile (Milinda uses rams butting and cymbals; deliberately not cited to avoid misquoting).
Day 1065 used Milinda's chariot; this day uses a different Milinda simile (the sauce).
